title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Histograms (geom_histogram)
Visualizing a single continuous variable:


ggplot(airquality, aes(x = Temp)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#3498db", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°F)", y = "Count")










Always test multiple binwidth values to avoid hiding peaks or creating artificial noise.

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Density Curves (geom_density)
Smooth probability density estimates:


ggplot(airquality, aes(x = Temp, fill = factor(Month))) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°F)", y = "Density", fill = "Month")










Use alpha = 0.4 so overlapping sub-populations remain visible.

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Boxplots (geom_boxplot)
Comparing distributions across categorical groups:


ggplot(airquality, aes(x = factor(Month), y = Ozone, fill = factor(Month))) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = 1, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Ozone (ppb)")










Displays 5-number summary (Min, Q1, Median, Q3, Max) + outlier flags.

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Boxplot + Jitter Overlay (geom_jitter)
Layering raw observations over boxplots reveals sample sizes and local clusters:


ggplot(airquality, aes(x = factor(Month), y = Ozone, fill = factor(Month))) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.5, color = "black")










Set outlier.shape = NA on the boxplot to prevent plotting outliers twice!

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Discrete Counts: geom_bar vs. geom_col


geom_bar() (Counts Rows)
When R calculates frequency for you:

# Data has raw individual rows
ggplot(airquality, aes(x = factor(Month))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue")


geom_col() (Pre-Summarized)
When data already has a numeric height column:

summary_df <- data.frame(
  region = c("North", "South", "West"),
  admissions = c(120, 340, 210))
ggplot(summary_df, aes(x = region, y = admissions)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkgreen")

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
geom_bar vs. geom_col: The Result


geom_bar(): R counts the rows










geom_col(): you supply the heights

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2

👥 Paired Exercise 2: Comparing Ozone by Month (10 min)

Pro-Tip
Layer order matters! Put geom_violin() first, then geom_boxplot() on top so the boxplot sits cleanly inside the violin body.

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Faceting with facet_wrap
Split complex multi-group data into clean sub-panels:

ggplot(airquality, aes(x = Temp, y = Ozone)) +
  geom_point(color = "navy", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ Month, nrow = 1)









nrow = 1 aligns all panels in a single horizontal strip.

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Controlling Facet Scales
By default, all subplots share the exact same axis limits (scales = "fixed"). Use scales = "free_y" for independent y-axes, or scales = "free" for fully independent axes:

ggplot(airquality, aes(x = Temp, y = Ozone)) +
  geom_point(color = "navy", alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ Month, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y")

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Free y-Scales: The Result















Note


Use fixed scales when comparing absolute quantities; use free scales when comparing internal distribution shapes.

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Informative Labels: labs()
Never leave raw column names on a presentation or report figure:

p_pub <- ggplot(airquality, aes(x = Temp, y = Ozone, color = Wind)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "black", linetype = "dashed", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Air Pollution Dynamics at LaGuardia Airport",
    subtitle = "Daily Ozone, Temperature, and Wind (May - Sep 1973)",
    x = "Maximum Daily Temperature (°F)",
    y = "Mean Ozone (ppb)",
    color = "Wind Speed\n(mph)",
    caption = "Source: NYS Department of Environmental Conservation"
  )
p_pub

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text: Informative Labels: labs()

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Colorblind-Safe Scales & Themes


Viridis Palettes

p_pub +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "viridis")









Perceptually uniform and legible in grayscale.


Clean Themes

p_pub +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "viridis") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Saving Figures: ggsave()
Save vector or high-resolution raster images for publications and reports:
ggsave(
  filename = "figures/figure1_ozone.png",
  plot = p_pub,
  width = 8,
  height = 5,
  dpi = 300
)

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Spotting Truncated Baselines


❌ AI Prompt: “Bar chart of mortality rate”

df <- data.frame(year = 2019:2023,
  rate = c(49.8, 50.1, 50.4, 50.2, 50.9))
ggplot(df, aes(x = year, y = rate)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(48, 52))


✅ The Verified Rule

# Same data, honest baseline at 0
ggplot(df, aes(x = year, y = rate)) +
  geom_col()

title: Week 4: Data Visualization with ggplot2
text:
Truncated vs. Honest Baseline


❌ Axis starts at 48










A truncated \(y\)-axis makes a 2% change look like a surge!


✅ Axis starts at 0










Bars must start at 0 (geom_col, geom_bar).
Overplotting: geom_jitter(), alpha < 0.5, or 2D density.
Color: colorblind-friendly scales (viridis).

title: Setup Guides
text:
The one-time checklist
You are fully set up when all five of these are true:

R and RStudio open, and git --version prints a version number in the RStudio Terminal tab.
You have a GitHub account, and you can sign in to it.
usethis::git_sitrep() shows your name, your email, and a stored GitHub token.
You can open a repository in RStudio and see a Git tab in the top-right pane.
You can commit a change and push it, and see it appear on github.com.

If any line fails, the guide that covers it is linked in the table above.

title: Setup Guides
text:
If you get stuck
Read the exact error message, then look it up on the error messages page. Nearly every Git problem people hit is one of about a dozen errors, and all of them are listed there with fixes.
If that does not resolve it, paste the exact error (or a screenshot) into an AI assistant and ask what it means. If you are still stuck after that, bring the error text to office hours or email it. Please do not spend an evening fighting the setup alone: it is not what this course is testing.






NoteNot in this course? Welcome anyway



These guides are written to stand on their own. Anything specific to GPH-GU 2182 is fenced off in a box labelled In this course; everything outside those boxes applies to any R user setting up Git and GitHub. You are welcome to link to these pages or adapt them for your own students.

title: Installing R, RStudio, and Git
text:
You need three separate pieces of software. They are easy to confuse, so it is worth being clear about what each one is:
Install them in that order: R first, then RStudio, then Git.

title: Installing R, RStudio, and Git
text:
1. Install R
Download it from cloud.r-project.org and run the installer with all the default options.

macOS: choose the .pkg that matches your chip. Apple Silicon (M1 through M4) needs the arm64 build; older Intel Macs need the x86_64 build. If you pick the wrong one, R will still install but some packages will fail to load later.
Windows: click “install R for the first time”, then download the .exe.

title: Installing R, RStudio, and Git
text:
2. Install RStudio
Download RStudio Desktop (the free open-source edition) from posit.co and install it with the defaults.
Open RStudio once. It should find R by itself and print a banner in the Console starting with R version, followed by whatever version you just installed. If RStudio opens but the Console is empty or complains that it cannot find R, R did not install correctly: reinstall it and then restart RStudio.
Quarto, which turns your .qmd files into documents, ships inside RStudio. You do not install it separately.

title: Installing R, RStudio, and Git
text:
3. Install Git

macOSWindowsLinux


Open the Terminal tab in RStudio (bottom-left pane, next to Console) and run:
xcode-select --install
A system dialog appears. Click Install and wait a few minutes. This installs Apple’s command line developer tools, which include Git.
If it says command line tools are already installed, you already have Git and you are done with this step.


Download Git for Windows from git-scm.com/download/win and run the installer.
Accept every default. The defaults matter more than they look: they put git on your system path, which is what lets RStudio find it. Do not change the editor or path options unless you know why you are changing them.
After it finishes, restart RStudio. RStudio only looks for Git when it starts, so a running RStudio will not notice the new installation.


sudo apt install git      # Debian, Ubuntu
sudo dnf install git      # Fedora

title: Installing R, RStudio, and Git
text:
4. Check that it worked
In RStudio, click the Terminal tab (bottom-left pane, beside Console) and type:
git --version
You want a version number back, such as git version 2.39.5. Any version is fine; Git is stable and old versions work. If you get command not found, see Git is not installed or RStudio cannot find it.
Then confirm RStudio itself knows where Git lives: Tools > Global Options > Git/SVN. The “Git executable” box should hold a real path (/usr/bin/git on macOS, something like C:/Program Files/Git/bin/git.exe on Windows) and Enable version control interface for RStudio projects should be checked.

text:
5. Install the R packages you will need
Paste this into the Console (the pane where R runs, not the Terminal) and press Enter:
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "usethis", "gitcreds"))
This takes several minutes the first time. Some output scrolls by in red; that is normal progress reporting, not an error. What matters is whether the final lines say the packages were unpacked and the prompt > comes back.
If you are asked “Do you want to install from sources the package which needs compilation?”, answer no unless you have a reason to compile.






TipIn this course



Add the course textbook package as well:
install.packages("r02pro")
That gives you the gm and sahp datasets used throughout the exercises.

title: Committing, pushing, and pulling
text:
Saving a file and saving your work are different things. Git puts three checkpoints between the file on your disk and the copy on GitHub, and almost every confusion about Git comes from collapsing them.








Step
What it does
Where the work now is




Save (Ctrl/Cmd+S)
Writes your edits to the file
On your disk only


Stage (tick the box)
Marks a file as part of the next snapshot
Chosen, not yet recorded


Commit
Records a permanent snapshot with a message
In your local history


Push
Uploads your commits to GitHub
On GitHub, visible to others



The consequence worth memorizing: a commit is not on GitHub until you push. Every term, someone commits diligently all week, never pushes, and believes the work was submitted. Only what is pushed exists to anyone but you.
Pull is the reverse of push: it brings down commits made elsewhere (by a collaborator, by your other laptop, or by an edit you made on github.com in the browser).

title: Committing, pushing, and pulling
text:
The routine
Once your project is open in RStudio, you will use the Git tab in the top-right pane. Files appear there as soon as they change.

1. Pull before you start
Click the blue Pull arrow. If you are the only person working, this usually reports “Already up to date”, which takes a second and saves you the rejected push described below.


2. Do your work, and save
Nothing Git-related here. Edit, save, run, render.


3. Stage what belongs in this snapshot
In the Git tab, tick the Staged checkbox next to each file you want to include. The two-letter status codes mean:







Code
Meaning




M
Modified: the file existed and you changed it


A
Added: a new file, now staged


?
Untracked: a new file Git has never seen (git status calls it ??)


D
Deleted


R
Renamed



Stage your source files. Do not stage things that are generated, huge, or private: see what not to commit.


4. Commit
Click Commit. A window opens showing your staged changes line by line, with additions in green and deletions in red. Read that diff: it is the cheapest bug check you will ever get.
Write a message in the box and click Commit.
A good message says what changed and why, in the present tense, in one line:

Good: Add Q3 boxplot and fix filter on year
Good: Correct sample size in the summary table
Less useful: update, stuff, asdf, final FINAL v2

You are writing to your future self, who will scroll this history in three months looking for the commit where something broke.


5. Push
Close the commit window and click the green Push arrow. When it finishes, your work is on GitHub.
If Push asks for a username and password, your token is not set up: go back to guide 2. If it reports that updates were rejected, click Pull first, then Push again.


6. Confirm
Open the repository on github.com and look at it. Your files should be there, with your commit message and a timestamp beside them. This takes five seconds and is the only real proof that the work is submitted.






TipIn this course



After you push, click the Actions tab on your repository page. Within about two minutes the autograder reports which questions passed. You can revise and push as often as you like before the deadline: only the final state counts, so a red X on an early attempt costs you nothing.

title: Committing, pushing, and pulling
text:
What not to commit
Git is for source, not for output or secrets.







Do commit
Do not commit




.R and .qmd files
Tokens, passwords, API keys


Small input data
Data you are not allowed to redistribute


.gitignore, README.md, .Rproj
Files over 100 MB (GitHub refuses them)


Anything needed to reproduce the work
.Rproj.user/, .Rhistory, .RData



A .gitignore file lists patterns Git should ignore, so those files stop appearing in the Git tab entirely. RStudio creates a sensible one for you when it makes a project. To add to it:
usethis::use_git_ignore(c("*.csv", "secrets.R"))






Important



Committing a secret and then deleting it does not remove it: it stays in the history and is still readable. If you push a token or password, revoke it immediately on GitHub and issue a new one. That is the fix; editing the file is not.

title: Committing, pushing, and pulling
section: The same thing in the Terminal
text:
The same thing in the Terminal
The Git tab is a friendly front end for a handful of commands. If you prefer typing, or you are on a machine without RStudio, these are the equivalents. Run them in the RStudio Terminal tab or any shell, from inside the project folder.
git status                        # what has changed, and what is staged
git add exercise.qmd              # stage one file
git add .                         # stage everything changed
git commit -m "Add Q3 boxplot"    # record a snapshot
git push                          # upload to GitHub
git pull                          # download from GitHub
git log --oneline                 # your history, one commit per line
git status is the single most useful command in Git. When you are lost, run it: it tells you where you are and usually suggests the command you want next.

title: Committing, pushing, and pulling
text:
Undoing things
Nothing here loses committed work. Git makes it genuinely hard to destroy something you have committed, which is most of the point of using it.








You want to
In RStudio
In the Terminal




Unstage a file
Untick its Staged box
git restore --staged FILE


Throw away uncommitted edits to a file
Git tab > select > More > Revert
git restore FILE


Fix the message on the last commit
Commit window > tick Amend previous commit
git commit --amend


See what changed in a file
Git tab > select > Diff
git diff FILE


Look at an old version
Git tab > History (clock icon)
git log -p FILE









Warning



Reverting uncommitted changes is the one genuinely destructive action in that table. Those edits were never recorded, so Git cannot bring them back. Commit first when you are unsure: a messy commit is always better than lost work.


Only amend a commit you have not pushed yet. Amending rewrites history, and rewriting history that others have already pulled creates a mess for them.

title: Committing, pushing, and pulling
section: When two people edit the same lines
text:
When two people edit the same lines
If you and a collaborator change the same lines of the same file, a pull produces a merge conflict. Git marks the disagreement inside the file:
<<<<<<< HEAD
mean_age <- mean(df$age, na.rm = TRUE)
=======
mean_age <- mean(df$age)
>>>>>>> origin/main
To resolve it: open the file, delete the three marker lines, keep the code you want (which may be a blend of both), save, then stage and commit as usual. The commit that follows is the resolution.
Conflicts are normal collaboration, not a failure. They are also much rarer when everyone pulls before starting and pushes when they finish.
